This isn't directly related to MakeMKV, but rather the optical drive itself, as this issue only crops up when I'm burning discs with tools like ImgBurn. Essentially what happens is, when the disc is done burning (DVD or BD, I haven't burned many CDs), when it does the "Cycle Tray before Verify" step, a good 50% of the time, instead of progressing normally, the drive gets locked in some sort of null state, where it never reports the disc being re-inserted. It hangs in such a way that any software that dares try to interact with the optical drive hangs or crashes. Only way to close ImgBurn in this state is through Task Manager, and if I try to open the drive in File Explorer, it crashes the entire explorer.exe process and the start menu disappears for a few minutes. Swapping out the disc with another or leaving the drive empty does not change the situation. The only fix is a full reboot - but even that gets interrupted - whether I Restart or Shut Down, the PC gets to the stage where it's no longer displaying anything and the monitor goes to sleep, but the PC continues to hang and never fully shuts down/reboots until I force it to with the restart or power buttons. If I take no direct action, the computer will simply never turn off, because the optical drive is preventing it from doing so. For context, this issue was present on Windows 10 and still on Windows 11, my machine has an Asus PRIME B350-M motherboard, Ryzen 7 5700X CPU, 16GB of RAM, and an RTX 3060 (though the issue was also present when I ran an ancient GTX 980). I did also used to have AnyDVD HD installed and currently have XReveal installed, though I never let these programs auto-run and the issue still happens on a fresh boot where XReveal has never been opened. I'm not sure if this is an issue with the motherboard - I keep the BIOS up to date and it's never fixed the problem - or the drive itself - I'm never upgrading the firmware if that's the only thing that would fix this bug, because it's a holy grail drive one of the last that came stock from the factory with the LibreDrive-compatible 1.03 firmware. It works great for ripping all manner of discs, and when it does burn and verify the results are consistent and very good, but this is a pretty major annoyance, and I was wondering if anyone else had dealt with it or knew of any fixes.
I've used ImgBurn for years and never heard of "Cycle Tray before Verify". Can't you just turn that off?

You've never heard of that? It's enabled by default and highly recommended. It's the thing where after burning a disc, the tray ejects and then closes again before it verifies the disc you just burned. I could turn it off if I didn't care about verifying my burns, but I do.

Can you provide a source regarding "LG" withdrawing from the Blu-ray drive market? I suspect you've confused LG (which manufactured Blu-ray players for TVs, until pulling out of the market in 2024 December) with Hitachi-LG Data Storage (a joint venture between Hitachi and LG, which manufactures optical drives for PCs, that carry "LG" branding). In my searches for tech news articles, I found plenty of articles discussing LG's withdrawal from the Blu-ray player market, and plenty of articles regarding Pioneer withdrawing from the PC optical drive market, but none of these articles mentioned HL-DT-ST. LG's withdrawal from the Blu-ray player market had no impact on HL-DT-ST. HL-DT-ST USB drives are still available at every retailer I checked. Several 3rd-party OEMs are also still selling optical drives based on HL-DT-ST's BU40N chipset (which is considered the best chipset HL-DT-ST has ever manufactured), such as the Verbatim 43888, and the ThinkPenguin TPE-BLUDVUSB3. Note that I can't find HL-DT-ST's 5.25 inch drives at any retailer. In one case, the retailer lists the BH16NS55 as "End of Life", and doesn't list any other 5.25 inch drives. I assume that HL-DT-ST has stopped manufacturing 5.25 inch drives, which isn't surprising, given that their 5.25 inch drives had a reputation on these forums for being vastly inferior to their USB drives. In my personal experience, the BH16NS55 regularly returns garbled data during prolonged or high-speed use, and often scratches Blu-ray discs in the process. With Pioneer no longer manufacturing optical drives, there's simply no reason why anyone should still go out of their way to build a desktop PC with 5.25 inch bays (PC cases with 5.25 inch bays are becoming increasingly rare and expensive), as opposed to just buying USB optical drives.

How The Patch Works What the problem was: The issue was that the INIC3639 (I assume) was initially designed not for ODDs but for SSDs - to be used in applications like M.2 or MSATA enclosures. Because of this this oversight and the fact that the programmers at Initio needed to be able to flash firmware to the USB to SATA converter, they hijacked the 0x3B (WRITE BUFFER) and 0x3C (READ BUFFER) SCSI opcodes completely. The problem with this, is that these opcodes are critical to flashing the ODD, and thus completely hijacking them breaks functionality. Based on testing, I am also highly certain that Libredrive also uses these opcodes for loading the temporary patch that allows it to function. How It works now: Instead of unconditionally diverting these commands to the bridge IC, as bridge-local vendor commands, the INIC3639 now forwards all commands other than 0x3C mode 0x01 (used to read the bridge’s 64-byte identity/configuration window) and 0x3B mode 0x10 (used to access the MPTool vendor channel) to the SATA interface which allows the MPTool to continue functioning properly and flashing and Libredrive to work correctly. How it was implemented: This was done by placing a 50 byte dispatcher in unused 0xFF padding.

Welcome to the forums [user], RPC-2 refers to the region coding used by DVD players, which can nowadays be trivially bypassed by using software like VLC Player that accesses the disk directly, using open source algorithms to bypass the CSS encryption used on DVDs. Video resolution varies from 720x576 (PAL) to 720x480 (NTSC). If this is your issue, then just using VLC Player is the simplest solution. Non-UHD Blu-ray players use a different (and much more complex) system called AACS (which has a different type of region coding where the world is split into 3 regions rather than 6 with DVD). VLC Player can be used to bypass this as well, but this requires extra setup (see the Bluray drive Doesn't work with VLC thread for more details). This should work with pretty much any BluRay drive and the video resolution of most HD content is 1920x1080. MakeMKV offers an alternative approach of making an unencrypted copy of your BluRay onto your hard disk, which you can then play without needing the disc (which should then be stored somewhere safe, away from any environmental hazards). For standard BluRay disks, it can handle most cases without the need for drive firmware flashing. However firmware flashing will enable a feature known as LibreDrive (see What is LibreDrive?) which can then handle any standard BluRay disc plus the enhanced protections used with UltraHD BluRays (video resolution 3840x2160, UHD discs have so far been region-free). For advice on flashable drives and how-tos, see the Ultimate UHD Drives Flashing Guide Updated 2026 thread. Be aware that most manufacture of UHD-capable drives stopped in 20224/2025 so remaining drives are much harder to get, are increasing rapidly in cost and there is an increasing number of fakes being sold. If you need to purchase a UHD-capable drive then it would be safest to check out the Drives for Sale forum, and to do so sooner rather than later.

FYI for anyone considering buying a new Archgon UHD drive from Amazon, the controller chip in that enclosure of late does not allow flashing. (H/T [user] - ... _archgons/ ) This drive: archgon Premium Aluminum External USB 3.0 UHD 4K Blu-Ray Writer Super Drive for PC and Mac I've acquired both old and new for kicks and grins to do some analysis. Comparisons: Package label: "MD-8107S-U3YC-UHD unit - USB Y cable - USB C cable - User Manual - Protective Case" (old) vs. "MD-8107S-U3YC-UHD unit - USB C + A cable - User Manual - Protective Case" (new) UPC code and all other text are identical Enclosure interface: Micro USB Type B SuperSpeed (old) vs. USB-C (new) Controller chip: initio INIC-3619PN (old) vs. initio INIC-3639PN (new) Serial number (less deterministic than the above 3 characteristics, but might be good info): 00070xxx (old) vs. 00093xxx (new) So if your Archgon enclosure has the above new characteristics, then you won't be able to flash. When running Marty McNuts SDF Flasher, clicking on Start doesn't do anything. You'll have to remove the drive and use some other means of flashing it (another enclosure with a different controller chip or a computer with a slimline SATA slot). To remove the drive, just take a small screwdriver and carefully remove the two back feet, which will reveal two screws, unscrew and slide out the drive in its mounting bracket and then the rest is simple.. Anyway, I made a detection program (Windows) if you want to use it to check: ArchgonUHDDetector.7z Or you can check which chip your Archgon is by going to Device Manager in Windows: Universal Serial Bus controllers > USB Mass Storage Device > Right-click for Properties > Details > Property dropdown - Hardware Ids USB\VID_13FD&PID_3910&REV_0217 (old) vs. USB\VID_13FD&PID_5910&REV_0157 (new) Hopefully this will help those who have purchased from Amazon so you can check it without opening the package or going too far and then you can just return it if you don't want it.

Hey everyone, I split my time between two countries, so I've ended up with a small fleet of drives rather than one setup I carry around. Mostly I'm ripping regular Blu-ray, with UHD less often, and I also burn BD-R/BD-R DL discs from the ripped files so my kids can grab a physical movie off the shelf instead of streaming, and to keep the originals protected. So for me, keeping burning solid matters just as much as keeping the ripping side working. Here's what I've got: In one country: a Verbatim 43888 (older stock with a Pioneer BDR-UD04 inside, still on stock 1.14, never flashed) paired with an OWC Mercury Pro that came with an LG WH16NS40, which I cross-flashed to WH16NS60 1.02-MK. In the other: a second Verbatim 43888 (same Pioneer setup, also stock), an ASUS SBW-06D5H-U with its BU40N flashed to 1.03-MK (carry in the backpack), and an ASUS BW-16D1X-U that I cross-flashed with the BW-16D1HT 3.10-MK firmware. The Verbatim/Pioneer pair I know not to patch — they're staying stock. My plan is actually to keep those two reserved for ripping, especially the tougher/problem discs, and deliberately not use them for burning BD-R DL, since I'd rather not put that kind of laser wear on them. So the LG-based drives are the ones that'll be doing the DL burning duty. Which is why I really want to nail down BD-R DL (the 50GB dual-layer discs) on those three. I've seen scattered reports around the forum of burns completing but failing verification right at the layer break, on a few different LG/MediaTek-platform drives, and I'd rather sort this out on paper than by burning through a stack of coasters (costly coasters ). So for the three flashed drives above: - Has anyone gotten clean, verified BD-R DL burns on WH16NS60 1.02-MK? - Same question for BU40N 1.03-MK? - And for BW-16D1HT 3.10-MK — is the layer-break issue baked into that platform regardless of firmware, or does 3.10-MK specifically hold up okay? If DL just isn't reliable on one or more of these no matter what, that's fine, I'll stick to single-layer BD-R on that drive. And I'm also open to just picking up an extra drive dedicated purely to burning, left on completely stock/untouched firmware, if that turns out to be the more reliable route for DL specifically — in which case, is there a drive currently known to handle BD-R DL cleanly out of the box, no flashing involved? Thanks for reading through all that — happy to report back with results if it's useful for anyone else in the same boat. Also, I already have a MakeMKV license, and honestly this project has been worth it many times over, so I'm planning to pick up a couple more licenses just to support the project further.
